narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

instructor.persona: A competitive Highland dance champion with a focus on historical accuracy.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance is associated with the 1746 Act of Proscription, which banned traditional Highland dress.
The name 'Seann Triubhas' translates to 'old trousers'.
While popular legend links the first steps to the act of kicking off restrictive breeches, researchers like D. G. MacLennan have clarified that these steps were later additions to the tradition.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is a primary event in global Highland dance competitions and is a standard requirement for dance theory exams.
It serves as a cultural expression of the Highland identity and the historical struggle against the suppression of traditional dress.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage — MISSING (use images)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers perform in either a '3 & 1' or '4 & 2' step configuration.
The dance begins with a mandatory first step, followed by a series of slow, brushing movements.
Upon a signal from the dancer, the music accelerates into a 'Quick Time' section, which features steps similar to the Highland Fling.
Watch for Brushing, Shedding.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is performed to the tune 'Whistle O'er the Lave o't'.
Historically, it was played on the fiddle, but it is now standard to perform it to bagpipe music.
Listen for the Bagpipes, Fiddle.
The tempo sits around 99 beats a minute.
The music transitions from a moderate, rhythmic tempo suitable for brushing movements to a significantly faster, driving pace that supports high-energy, percussive footwork.

scenes.title: The people
narration: D. G. MacLennan, Elizabeth Grant, Margaret Gillis, Frank Rhodes, G. Douglas Taylor, William Cameron, Joan & Tom Flett.
A percussive version was documented in Cape Breton, Nova Scotia, by Frank Rhodes in 1957, which could be danced to the 'Irish Washerwoman' jig.
The dance is a recognized form of Scottish Highland dance, sharing technical elements with the Highland Fling.
